name: Jade Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Jade. I'm from the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to tech firms, employers, unions or government, and your answers stay confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on a cardiac step-down unit, so patients who've come out of coronary care but still need watching, mostly after stents or heart attacks. I usually have five patients, all on heart monitors, and I spend the day doing obs, titrating drips, teaching people about their new tablets and calming down very frightened husbands. The hospital got bought by a private chain two years ago, and since then everything is about 'flow'.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the teaching part, when a man who thought his life was over learns to check his own pulse and goes home with a plan. What drains me is the managers from head office who've never touched a patient asking why our discharges are slow. And night shifts, which I'm getting too old for at twenty-seven, apparently.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about home.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Selin, who's a freelance graphic designer. We've been saving for a house deposit for four years and we've got a good chunk put away, plus I'm on the higher end of pay for a ward nurse because of the cardiac allowance. Selin's work has been patchy this year, though, so I'm quietly the steady one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Okay, that's a world I can picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what most nurses already say, which is that the robots were never coming for us. I'd maybe post something sarcastic about all the money the chain wasted on AI pilots. At work I'd keep pushing the union line that the real problem is staffing, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my bigger worry is the chain and Selin's work, not AI. The chain will keep cutting corners whatever happens with technology. And Selin's clients were already shrinking before anyone said AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the unit and keep paying into the house fund every month, about six hundred. I'd go to the union meeting about the chain's new rota, because that's the fight in front of me. I might help Selin chase a few more clients through friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, honestly, but about the usual stuff. The chain and money for the house, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Selin's work was shrinking before AI. What's behind that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Clients cutting budgets, mostly, and a couple who moved to cheaper designers online. Even if AI turns out to be hype, my partner Selin is still losing design clients, and I'm still the one paying most of the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a routine task on your unit you'd happily see a machine do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Monitor alarms. Half of them are a loose lead or someone scratching their chest. If a system could sort the real arrhythmias from the junk, I'd hug it.

say: I'd say robots were **never coming** for nurses in the first place.
I'd joke online about the **money the chain wasted** on AI pilots.
think: My real worry is the **private chain** cutting corners, whatever technology does.
I know **Selin's clients** were already shrinking before AI came up at all.
do: Keep paying about **600 a month** into the house deposit fund.
Go to the **union meeting** on the chain's new rota plans.
Help Selin find **new design clients** through friends and old colleagues.
feel: **Uneasy** about ordinary pressures: the hospital owners and the household money.
S0.quote: Even if AI turns out to be hype, my partner Selin is still losing design clients, and I'm still the one paying most of the rent.
fieldNote: Her unease in a quiet world comes from her **partner's income**, not her own job.
She blames the **for-profit owners** more than any technology for the ward's problems.
She'd welcome a machine that filters **false monitor alarms**, a concrete, small wish.

steps.text: Pay 600 a month into the joint house deposit fund
Attend the union meeting on the chain's new rota

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one feels real. Like that's already starting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nurses are mostly fine but the people around us aren't. At work I'd back the union asking for a say in any AI rollout. Online I'd probably share stuff about designers and writers losing work, because that's Selin's world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, the charting and care-plan stuff gets automated and my day changes, but I keep my job. For Selin, it's worse. If AI does logos and layouts, her freelance income could halve, and we'd be living on mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once other units had tried the new charting tools and they worked, I'd learn them properly. We'd pause the house hunt for a year and keep the deposit in savings. I'd also push up how much we save, maybe from six hundred to eight hundred a month, by cutting takeaways and the weekend trips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious for Selin, and a bit guilty, because I'm basically fine. Tired at the thought of more change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Selin the night you realised her income was going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time and we've got the deposit, so nobody needs to panic. I'd tell my partner Selin that the house deposit can be our safety net for a year, and the house can wait. Then I'd probably cry in the shower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the tools once others had tried them. How would you know they'd worked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the nurses on the respiratory ward stopped complaining about them, honestly. That's my test. I'd wait about six months and then ask.

say: I'd say nurses are **mostly fine**, but people around them are losing **work**.
I'd back the union's call for a **say** in any **AI rollout** at the hospital.
think: My **charting** changes, but my job stays; for Selin it's much worse.
If AI does logos and layouts, **Selin's income** could halve and we'd live on mine.
do: Learn the **new charting tools** once other units show they work, after about six months.
**Pause the house hunt** for a year and keep the deposit as savings.
Raise monthly saving from 600 to **800** by cutting takeaways and weekend trips.
feel: **Anxious** for Selin and guilty that her own job is safe.
**Tired** at the thought of yet more change at work.
S1.quote: I'd tell my partner Selin that the house deposit can be our safety net for a year, and the house can wait.
fieldNote: The household's risk sits with her **freelance partner**, which pushes her mood up a notch.
Her test for new tools is plainly social: **wait until colleagues** stop complaining.
She turns the **house deposit** into a safety net, a big change for a couple saving four years.

steps.text: Ask respiratory ward nurses about the charting tool, then learn it properly
Put the house hunt on hold for a year
Cut takeaways and weekend trips to save 800 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. God. Selin first, then me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is why we need governments to step in, with income support and rules on robots in hospitals. At work I'd be loud in the union about staffing laws before 2031. Online I'd share every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, by 2028 Selin's design work is pretty much gone. Then I'm the only income, and three years later robots that can lift and turn patients turn up. By 2031 a robot can turn my patients, and by then I'd be the only earner in a house we haven't bought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the house plan completely and keep the whole deposit liquid. I'd pick up extra shifts while they're still there, maybe two a month, and push the union hard on safe-staffing laws. I'd help Selin look at retraining, maybe into something hands-on, which feels mad to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the floor is moving. Angry too, that it's all happening so fast nobody gets a say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between AI and robots mean for your unit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means 2028 to 2031 the computer does the care plans, the drug calculations, the discharge letters, and I just do the hands-on stuff. That's maybe half my day. Then the robots come for the other half, and I don't know what's left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You have a strong cushion. Does it make the two years feel any different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It buys us maybe eighteen months if we both lost everything. That's not nothing. But it doesn't fix the fact that every hospital would be cutting at the same time.

say: I'd call for **government income support** and rules on hospital robots.
I'd push the union loudly for **safe-staffing laws** before 2031.
think: I expect **Selin's design work** to be mostly gone by 2028.
I'd be the **only earner** just as robots arrive for my patients in 2031.
do: **Stop the house plan** completely and keep the whole deposit in easy-access savings.
Take **two extra shifts** a month while they still exist.
Help Selin look at **retraining** into hands-on work.
feel: **Alarmed**, as if the floor is moving under the household.
**Angry** that change comes too fast for anyone to have a say.
S2.quote: By 2031 a robot can turn my patients, and by then I'd be the only earner in a house we haven't bought.
fieldNote: She expects a **household earner** to lose most income, which makes this alarmed, not anxious.
Savings buy about **eighteen months**, which she counts precisely and doesn't oversell.
She sees half her day as **thinking work** that goes in 2028, the rest in 2031.

steps.text: Cancel the house purchase and keep the deposit in easy-access savings
Pick up two extra shifts a month on the step-down unit
Lobby the union for a national safe-staffing law before 2031
Help Selin apply for retraining grants into hands-on work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast, but at least you'd see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to plan it properly, so the government had better. I'd keep up the union stuff about robots counting toward staffing. With friends I'd say nurses are in a better place than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means Selin can start moving now, before the design market collapses. And I get time to get good at the AI side of cardiac nursing, so I'm the one who supervises the systems, not the one replaced. We might still buy the house if we're careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the hospital's digital nursing training once the first group had been through it. I'd keep saving eight hundred a month and look at a cheaper house further out. I'd vote for whoever promised proper transition support, and I'd say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more in control. Like I've been given a head start in a race I didn't enter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd supervise the systems. What does that look like on your unit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking what the AI flags on the monitors, signing off its drug plans, being the human who explains it to patients. I'd rather be the nurse who checks the computer's work than the nurse the computer replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've gone back to the house idea. What changed between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means a mortgage term doesn't look insane. We'd buy something smaller, maybe a two-bed flat instead of a house, so we could pay it on my income alone if we had to.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to plan**, so the **government** should act.
I'd tell friends nurses are in a **better place** than most workers.
think: Five years lets Selin **move careers** before the design market collapses.
I could become the nurse who **supervises the AI**, rather than the one replaced.
do: Join the hospital's **digital nursing training** after the first group finishes.
Look for a **smaller two-bed flat** we could afford on one income.
**Vote** for whoever promises proper transition support, and say so publicly.
feel: **Anxious**, but more in control, like getting a head start.
S3.quote: I'd rather be the nurse who checks the computer's work than the nurse the computer replaces.
fieldNote: Extra time changes her from defending to **planning a role**, supervising AI on the unit.
She sizes the **home purchase** to one income, a clear sign she expects Selin's work to fade.
Her steady style shows: she'd join training only **after the first group**.

steps.text: Join the second group of the hospital's digital nursing course
Buy a smaller two-bed flat payable on one nurse's salary
Vote for the party promising the strongest worker transition support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay. I can breathe with that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time to do this fairly, and if workers still get dumped it's a political choice. I'd say that at union meetings and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd be okay. Selin has time to retrain properly, maybe into teaching art, and I'd have time to specialise. With ten years' warning, my partner Selin can retrain properly and I can become the cardiac specialist nurse nobody wants to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the cardiac rehab specialist course in the next two years. We'd buy the house within a year, since there's time to pay a good chunk off before 2036. Selin would start a part-time teaching qualification while still taking design jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. Hopeful even. The end point still bothers me, but there's room to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why cardiac rehab in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's mostly talking people through fear and teaching them to trust their own heart again. A robot can lift a patient, but I don't think a heart attack survivor wants a robot telling them it's safe to have sex again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said if workers get dumped it's a political choice. Who would you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Governments that let hospital chains bank all the savings. And the chain I work for, honestly, because they'd take every robot they could get and call it innovation.

say: I'd say a **decade** is enough to do this fairly, so dumping workers is a **political choice**.
I'd say this at **union meetings** and online.
think: I think we'd be **okay**, with time for Selin to **retrain** into art teaching.
I'd have time to **specialise**, becoming a nurse nobody wants to replace.
do: Start the **cardiac rehab specialist** course within the next two years.
**Buy the house** within a year and pay down a good chunk before 2036.
Support Selin starting a **part-time teaching qualification** while still designing.
feel: Mostly **calm** and even **hopeful**, though the end point still bothers her.
S4.quote: With ten years' warning, my partner Selin can retrain properly and I can become the cardiac specialist nurse nobody wants to replace.
fieldNote: With a decade, her household plan has **two careers** moving, not one defending.
She blames **governments and the chain** for any harm, not the technology.
She picks rehab for its **emotional teaching**, which she sees as hardest to automate.

steps.text: Enrol in the cardiac rehab specialist nursing course by 2028
Buy the house within a year and overpay the mortgage
Help Selin fit a part-time teaching qualification around design work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Selin's work goes first and I'm left holding everything just as the robots arrive. What would help is real income support while people retrain, and rules saying robots on wards are there to help nurses, not replace them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how couples split the risk. Everyone asks if their own job is safe, but it's the house that has to survive. My job might be safe from robots for years, but my household isn't, because my partner's work goes first.

headlineQuote: My job might be safe from robots for years, but my household isn't, because my partner's work goes first.
portrait: Jade is a **27-year-old** cardiac step-down nurse at a hospital owned by a **private chain**.
She lives with partner Selin, a **freelance designer**, and they've saved a house deposit for four years.
She adopts new tools only once **colleagues have tested** them, and blames owners rather than technology.
Her mood follows **Selin's income**: anxious in Steady Disruption and alarmed in AGI by 2028.
With ten years, she'd **specialise** in cardiac rehab and buy the house after all.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, where Selin's income goes first and Jade becomes the **only earner** before robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** for people while they retrain.
Rules saying ward robots **help nurses** rather than replace them.
